rv.q: Act 2 of "Bust" is mostly excellent, especially the scenes where the actor Keith Randolph Smith, who I've admired for decades, lays out the price always paid by Black Americans, whether engaged in an assaultive world or choosing to inhabit somewhere different, somewhere of their own design.
“Bust” punches deep into the physical and emotional devastation that invariably results when all-consuming anger has no outlet.
Overall, BUST gives audiences many questions to ponder: Both in terms of unveiling the play’s unique building, but also when it comes to unpacking the themes and what to take away.
The writing, directing and acting is superb!
Zora Howard’s new play deals with a people’s rages through the ages.
Hilarious, thrilling and thought-provoking, “Bust” is a must-see for those who seek the examined life.

An all-too-familiar story with a fantastical twist, “Bust,” co-produced by Goodman Theatre and Atlanta’s Alliance Theatre, in association with Sonia Friedman Productions, is a visceral, disquieting yet funny tale.

As it stands, "Bust" is a piece with two distinct voices: one that speaks in the language of humor, pain, and communal survival, and another that whispers through metaphor, without always being heard.
Still, I wonder how powerful her message could have been if one word, one volatile connotation to provoke rage, was removed.
The performance is an immaculately staged, intricately conceived and hell-raising address to the agony of institutionalized racism in Huntsville, Alabama and the limberlost.
This becomes a special work of art rather than just another play.

cn.t: Critics praise Howard's imaginative and provocative world premiere, celebrating its bold exploration of racism and rage through a unique blend of mystery, drama, and speculative elements that defies easy categorization.
